Pfaffian–Toeplitz identities, Schur positivity, and the qq-log-convexity of Baxter polynomials

Yanxin Liu Email: liu-yanxin@outlook.com    Jianxi Mao Email: maojx@dlut.edu.cn Address: School of Mathematical Sciences, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian 116024,
P. R. China Corresponding author: Corresponding author
Abstract

We use the Pfaffian minor summation formula together with Jacobi–Trudi Toeplitz matrices to derive Pfaffian expansions in skew Schur functions. This yields explicit Schur expansions for several generating functions involving products of skew Schur functions. In particular, using sparse skew-symmetric matrices, we provide a Pfaffian proof of a Schur-positive identity arising in the study of the qq-log-convexity of the Narayana polynomials. As the main application, we prove that the Baxter polynomials form a qq-log-convex sequence. We further show that the Baxter transformation defined by the refined Baxter numbers preserves log-convexity. Finally, by realizing the qq-refined Baxter numbers as principal specializations of rectangular Schur functions, we prove that the array of qq-refined Baxter numbers is qq-log-concave both along each row and along each column. Both qq-log-concavity results extend naturally to the qq-analogues of the dd-Hoggatt numbers.

Keywords: 
Pfaffians , Schur functions , Baxter numbers , Log-convexity, qq-Log-convexity
2020 MSC
05E05, 15A15 , 05A15

Contents

 

1 Introduction

The aim of this article is twofold. The first is to combine the Pfaffian minor summation formula with skew Jacobi–Trudi Toeplitz matrices to obtain skew Schur expansions of certain symmetric functions. The second is to use these Schur-positive identities to prove the qq-log-convexity of the Baxter polynomials.

A matrix M=[Mi​j]1≤i,j≤2​nM=[M_{ij}]_{1\leq i,j\leq 2n} is called skew-symmetric if Mi​j=−Mj​iM_{ij}=-M_{ji} for all i,ji,j. The Pfaffian of a skew-symmetric matrix MM, denoted by Pf⁡(M)\Pf(M), is explicitly defined by the formula

Pf⁡(M)=12n​n!​∑σ∈𝔖2​nsgn⁡(σ)​∏i=1nMσ⁡(2​i−1),σ⁡(2​i),\Pf(M)=\frac{1}{2^{n}n!}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{2n}}\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^{n}M_{\sigma(2i-1),\sigma(2i)},

where 𝔖2​n\mathfrak{S}_{2n} is the symmetric group of degree 2​n2n and sgn⁡(σ)\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma) is the signature of σ\sigma.

Pfaffian methods have numerous applications in the theory of symmetric functions and related areas [15, 17, 19, 23, 25, 34, 40]. In particular, Ishikawa and Wakayama [20] established the Pfaffian minor summation formula. Let [m]:={1,2,…,m}[m]:=\{1,2,\ldots,m\} and let MI,JM_{I,J} be the submatrix of MM obtained by selecting the rows and columns indexed by II and JJ.

Lemma 1.1.

([20, Theorem 1]) Let m≤nm\leq n and mm be even. Suppose that HH is an m×nm\times n matrix, and Ω\Omega is an n×nn\times n skew-symmetric matrix. Then H​Ω​H𝖳H\Omega H^{\mathsf{T}} is a skew-symmetric matrix and

Pf⁡(H​Ω​H𝖳)=∑J⊂[n]|J|=mdetH[m],J​Pf⁡(ΩJ,J).\Pf\left(H\Omega H^{\mathsf{T}}\right)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}J\subset[n]\\ |J|=m\end{subarray}}\det H_{[m],J}\Pf\left(\Omega_{J,J}\right). (1)

This Pfaffian minor summation formula and its specializations have been used to derive a variety of identities for Schur functions and related symmetric functions [22, 23, 24]. For example, Sundquist [41] proved two-variable generalizations of this formula and applied them to express Schur functions in terms of Pfaffians. Bump and Diaconis [5] further explored the close connection between symmetric functions and Toeplitz matrices. Okada [34] gave Pfaffian analogues of the Cauchy–Binet formulas that provide direct proofs of many basic identities for Schur QQ-functions. Huh et al. [18] used the Pfaffian minor summation formula to establish affine bounded Littlewood identities for cylindric Schur functions.

Ishikawa, Okada and Wakayama [21] developed a systematic application of the Pfaffian minor summation formula to identities involving Schur polynomials. By specializing the matrix HH in (1) to a Vandermonde-type matrix, they expressed weighted Schur series as Pfaffians.

In this paper, we develop a Pfaffian method for Schur positivity by combining the Pfaffian minor summation formula with Jacobi–Trudi Toeplitz matrices. The Toeplitz formulation allows us to choose sparse skew-symmetric matrices whose Pfaffians can be evaluated directly. The minor summation expansion gives an explicitly Schur-positive series. Equating the two expressions produces nontrivial Schur-positive identities. As a first illustration, we obtain a Pfaffian proof of the identity used by Chen, Wang and Yang [7] in their proof of the qq-log-convexity of the Narayana polynomials. Further specializations give two additional identities, and we use them to prove the qq-log-convexity of the Baxter polynomials.

Let (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} be a sequence of nonnegative numbers. The sequence is called log-concave (resp. log-convex) if an2≥an−1​an+1a_{n}^{2}\geq a_{n-1}a_{n+1} (resp. an2≤an−1​an+1a_{n}^{2}\leq a_{n-1}a_{n+1}) for all n≥1n\geq 1. Log-concave and log-convex sequences often arise in combinatorics, algebra and geometry; see, for example,  [4, 13, 30, 38]. For a polynomial f⁡(q)∈ℝ⁡[q]f(q)\in\mathbb{R}[q], write f(q)≥q0f(q)\geq_{q}0 if it has only nonnegative coefficients. A polynomial sequence (fn​(q))n≥0(f_{n}(q))_{n\geq 0} is called qq-log-concave if

fn(q)2−fn−1(q)fn+1(q)≥q0,n≥1,f_{n}(q)^{2}-f_{n-1}(q)f_{n+1}(q)\geq_{q}0,\quad n\geq 1,

and it is called qq-log-convex if

fn−1(q)fn+1(q)−fn(q)2≥q0,n≥1.f_{n-1}(q)f_{n+1}(q)-f_{n}(q)^{2}\geq_{q}0,\quad n\geq 1.

The notion of qq-log-concavity goes back to Stanley. Sagan [35, 36] established the qq-log-concavity of sequences of symmetric functions and investigated the qq-log-concavity of the qq-binomial coefficients. Liu and Wang [30] introduced the notion of qq-log-convexity, and proved that some well-known polynomials such as Bell polynomials and Eulerian polynomials are qq-log-convex. The notion of qq-log-convexity has been extensively studied [7, 8, 43, 44, 45]. In particular, using the theory of Schur positivity, Chen, Wang and Yang [7] proved the (strong) qq-log-convexity of Narayana polynomials.

The principal application in this paper concerns the Baxter numbers. Baxter numbers enumerate Baxter permutations, which originated in Baxter’s study [1] of fixed points for the composite of commuting functions. Chung et al. [9] presented a sum formula for the Baxter numbers BnB_{n}, where

Bn=∑k=0nB⁡(n,k)=∑k=0n(nk)​(n+1k)​(n+2k)(k+1k)​(k+2k),0≤k≤n.B_{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}B(n,k)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{\binom{n}{k}\binom{n+1}{k}\binom{n+2}{k}}{\binom{k+1}{k}\binom{k+2}{k}},\quad 0\leq k\leq n.

We call B⁡(n,k)B(n,k) the refined Baxter number.

The Baxter numbers and Baxter permutations are of great significance in combinatorics, algebra and analysis [12, 28, 32]. Various bijections involving Baxter permutations have been constructed [11, 29]. Fang, Zhang and Zhao [14] provided an analytic study of Baxter numbers. Dilks [12] developed a comprehensive and unified study of Baxter objects, including the involutions, the (−1)(-1)-phenomenon and gamma-nonnegativity. It is known [10] that the binomial coefficients, the Narayana numbers and the refined Baxter numbers can be viewed as specializations of the dd-Hoggatt numbers with d=1,2,3d=1,2,3, respectively. The second author and Shi [33] studied the log-behavior of the dd-Hoggatt numbers.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the necessary background on symmetric functions. In Section 3, we combine the Pfaffian minor summation formula with skew Jacobi–Trudi Toeplitz matrices to derive several Schur function identities. Section 4 introduces the qq-refined Baxter numbers and interprets refined Baxter numbers and their q-analogues via rectangular Schur specializations. In Section 5, we establish a Schur positivity theorem and use it to prove the qq-log-convexity of the Baxter polynomials. Section 6 presents several further log-behavior properties associated with the refined Baxter numbers. We first show that the Baxter transformation preserves log-convexity. Then we prove the qq-log-concavity of the qq-refined Baxter numbers both along each fixed row and along each fixed column and extend these results to the qq-analogues of the dd-Hoggatt numbers. The appendices contain several auxiliary symmetric function identities and computational details used in the proofs.

2 Background

In this section, we give an overview of relevant background on symmetric functions. Throughout this paper, we adopt the notation and terminology for partitions and symmetric functions in Stanley [39]. Given a nonnegative integer nn, a partition λ\lambda of nn is a weakly decreasing nonnegative integer sequence (λ1,λ2,…,λk)(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k}) such that ∑i=1kλi=n\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}=n. The number of nonzero parts λi\lambda_{i} is called the length of λ\lambda, denoted by ℓ⁡(λ)\ell(\lambda). We write imii^{m_{i}} to indicate that the part ii occurs mim_{i} times in λ\lambda.

The Young diagram of λ\lambda is a left-justified array of cells with ℓ⁡(λ)\ell(\lambda) rows and λi\lambda_{i} cells in row ii. Transposing the diagram of λ\lambda, we get the conjugate partition of λ\lambda, denoted λ′\lambda^{\prime}. A cell (i,j)(i,j) is the cell in row ii and column jj. The hook length of (i,j)(i,j), denoted h⁡(i,j)h(i,j), is given by

h⁡(i,j)=λi+λj′−i−j+1.h(i,j)=\lambda_{i}+\lambda_{j}^{\prime}-i-j+1.

The content of (i,j)(i,j), denoted c⁡(i,j)c(i,j), is given by c⁡(i,j)=j−i.c(i,j)=j-i.

Given two partitions λ\lambda and μ\mu, we say that λ\lambda contains μ\mu, denoted μ⊆λ\mu\subseteq\lambda, if λi≥μi\lambda_{i}\geq\mu_{i} for each ii. When μ⊆λ\mu\subseteq\lambda, we can define a skew partition λ/μ\lambda/\mu as the diagram obtained from the diagram of λ\lambda by removing the cells in the top-left corner corresponding to the diagram of μ\mu.

A semistandard Young tableau of shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is an array T=[Ti​j]T=[T_{ij}] of positive integers of shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu that is weakly increasing in every row and strictly increasing down every column. The type of TT is defined as the composition α=(α1,α2,…)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\ldots), where αi\alpha_{i} is the number of ii’s in TT. Let XX denote the set of variables {x1,x2,…}\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots\}. If TT has type α\alpha, then we write

XT=x1α1x2α2⋯.X^{T}=x_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}x_{2}^{\alpha_{2}}\cdots.

The skew Schur function sλ/μ​(X)s_{\lambda/\mu}(X) of shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu is defined as the generating function

sλ/μ​(X)=∑TXT,s_{\lambda/\mu}(X)=\sum_{T}X^{T},

over all semistandard Young tableaux TT of shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu filled with positive integers. When μ\mu is the empty partition ∅\varnothing, we call sλ​(X)s_{\lambda}(X) the Schur function of shape λ\lambda. We set s∅​(X)=1s_{\emptyset}(X)=1. Throughout this paper, we adopt the convention that sλ=0s_{\lambda}=0 whenever λ\lambda does not define a valid partition.

A symmetric function ff is called Schur positive if the coefficients aλa_{\lambda} in the expansion f=∑λaλ​sλf=\sum_{\lambda}a_{\lambda}s_{\lambda} are all nonnegative, and we denote [sλ]​f=aλ.\left[s_{\lambda}\right]f=a_{\lambda}.

For a Schur function sλs_{\lambda}, define the standard involution ω⁡(sλ)=sλ′\omega(s_{\lambda})=s_{\lambda^{\prime}}, where λ′\lambda^{\prime} is the conjugate partition of λ\lambda. Let f,gf,g be two symmetric functions and a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}. Then

ω⁡(a​f+b​g)=a​ω​(f)+b​ω​(g)andω⁡(f​g)=ω⁡(f)​ω​(g).\omega(af+bg)=a\omega(f)+b\omega(g)\quad\textrm{and}\quad\omega(fg)=\omega(f)\omega(g).
Lemma 2.1.

Let ff be a symmetric function. Then ff is Schur positive if and only if ω⁡(f)\omega(f) is Schur positive.

Let Y={y1,y2,…}Y=\{y_{1},y_{2},\ldots\} be another set of variables, and let sλ/μ​(X,Y)s_{\lambda/\mu}(X,Y) denote the skew Schur function in X∪YX\cup Y. The following basic property will be used later:

sλ/μ​(X,Y)=∑νsλ/ν​(X)​sν/μ​(Y),s_{\lambda/\mu}(X,Y)=\sum_{\nu}s_{\lambda/\nu}(X)s_{\nu/\mu}(Y), (2)

where the sum ranges over all partitions ν\nu satisfying μ⊆ν⊆λ\mu\subseteq\nu\subseteq\lambda; see [39, Section 7].

Let

ek​(X)=∑i1<…<ikxi1​…​xike_{k}(X)=\sum_{i_{1}<\ldots<i_{k}}x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{k}}

be the elementary symmetric functions with e0=1e_{0}=1 and ek=0e_{k}=0 for k<0k<0; and let

hk​(X)=∑i1≤…≤ikxi1​…​xikh_{k}(X)=\sum_{i_{1}\leq\ldots\leq i_{k}}x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{k}}

be the complete homogeneous symmetric functions with h0=1h_{0}=1 and hk=0h_{k}=0 for k<0k<0. Then

ek​(X)=s(1k)​(X)andhk​(X)=s(k)​(X).e_{k}(X)=s_{(1^{k})}(X)\quad\textrm{and}\quad h_{k}(X)=s_{(k)}(X).

The skew Jacobi–Trudi identity (see [39, Theorem 7.16.1]) expresses the skew Schur function sλ/μs_{\lambda/\mu} as a determinant of complete homogeneous symmetric functions,

sλ/μ=det(hλi−μj−i+j)1≤i,j≤ℓ⁡(λ).s_{\lambda/\mu}=\det(h_{\lambda_{i}-\mu_{j}-i+j})_{1\leq i,j\leq\ell(\lambda)}. (3)

Note that for a two-row partition λ=(a,b)\lambda=(a,b) and μ=∅\mu=\varnothing, where a≥ba\geq b, the Jacobi–Trudi identity gives

s(a,b)=det[haha+1hb−1hb]=ha​hb−ha+1​hb−1.s_{(a,b)}=\det\begin{bmatrix}h_{a}&h_{a+1}\\ h_{b-1}&h_{b}\end{bmatrix}=h_{a}h_{b}-h_{a+1}h_{b-1}. (4)

Recall that a lattice permutation of length nn is a sequence w1w2⋯wnw_{1}w_{2}\cdots w_{n} such that for any ii and jj in the subsequence w1w2⋯wjw_{1}w_{2}\cdots w_{j} the number of ii’s is greater than or equal to the number of i+1i+1’s. Let TT be a semistandard Young tableau. The reverse reading word TrevT^{\mathrm{rev}} is a sequence of entries of TT obtained by first reading each row from right to left and then concatenating the rows from top to bottom. If the reverse reading word TrevT^{\mathrm{rev}} is a lattice permutation, we call TT a Littlewood–Richardson tableau. The Littlewood–Richardson rule enables us to expand a product of Schur functions in terms of Schur functions. Given two Schur functions sμs_{\mu} and sνs_{\nu}, Littlewood–Richardson coefficients cμ,νλc_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda} are defined by the following relation

sμ​sν=∑λcμ,νλ​sλ,s_{\mu}s_{\nu}=\sum_{\lambda}c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}s_{\lambda}, (5)

where cμ,νλc_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda} is the number of Littlewood–Richardson tableaux of shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu and content ν\nu [39, A1.5]. For example, if λ=(4,3,1),μ=(2,1),ν=(3,2)\lambda=(4,3,1),\,\mu=(2,1),\,\nu=(3,2), then cμ,νλ=2c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}=2. Indeed, there are two Littlewood–Richardson tableaux of shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu and content ν\nu as shown in Figure 1.

When ν=(k)\nu=(k) or ν=(1k)\nu=(1^{k}) in (5), the Littlewood–Richardson rule has a simpler description, known as Pieri’s rule. We need the notion of horizontal and vertical strips. A skew partition λ/μ\lambda/\mu is called a horizontal (or vertical) strip of size kk if there are kk cells in total with no two cells lying in the same column (resp. in the same row).

Theorem 2.2.

[39, Theorem 7.15.7, Corollary 7.15.9] We have

sμ​hk=∑λsλ,s_{\mu}h_{k}=\sum_{\lambda}s_{\lambda},

summed over all partitions λ\lambda such that λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a horizontal strip of size kk, and

sμ​ek=∑λsλ,s_{\mu}e_{k}=\sum_{\lambda}s_{\lambda},

summed over all partitions λ\lambda such that λ/μ\lambda/\mu is a vertical strip of size kk.

3 Main results

In this section, we combine the Pfaffian minor summation formula (1) with Jacobi–Trudi Toeplitz matrices to derive some identities involving symmetric functions. We first recall some basic properties of Pf⁡(M)\Pf(M); see [27].

Lemma 3.1.

Let M=[Mi​j]1≤i,j≤2​nM=[M_{ij}]_{1\leq i,j\leq 2n} be a skew-symmetric matrix.

  • (i)

    For a fixed row index ii, if Mi​j=0M_{ij}=0 for 1≤j≤2​n,1\leq j\leq 2n, then Pf⁡(M)=0\Pf(M)=0.

  • (ii)

    The first-row expansion formula for the Pfaffian is

    Pf⁡(M)=∑j=22​n(−1)j​M1​j​Pf⁡(M[2​n]∖{1,j},[2​n]∖{1,j}).\Pf(M)=\sum_{j=2}^{2n}(-1)^{j}M_{1j}\Pf\left(M_{[2n]\setminus\{1,j\},[2n]\setminus\{1,j\}}\right).

Recall that hkh_{k} is the kk-th complete homogeneous symmetric function. Let mm be a positive integer and μ\mu be a partition with ℓ⁡(μ)≤m\ell(\mu)\leq m. Define the row–truncated Toeplitz matrix

Hμ(m)=[hj−i−μm−i+1]1≤i≤m,j≥1.H^{(m)}_{\mu}=\bigl[h_{j-i-\mu_{m-i+1}}\bigr]_{1\leq i\leq m,\ j\geq 1}.

Define H(m)=H∅(m).H^{(m)}=H^{(m)}_{\varnothing}. The following is a corollary of the skew Jacobi–Trudi identity.

Lemma 3.2.

Let J={j1,…,jm}<J=\{j_{1},\ldots,j_{m}\}_{<}. Then we have

det(Hμ(m))[m],J=sλ/μ,\det\left(H^{(m)}_{\mu}\right)_{[m],J}=s_{\lambda/\mu},

where λ=(jm−m,jm−1−(m−1),…,j1−1)\lambda=\bigl(j_{m}-m,j_{m-1}-(m-1),\ldots,j_{1}-1\bigr).

Proof.

Let H=Hμ(m)H=H_{\mu}^{(m)}. By definition,

H[m],{j1,j2,⋯,jm}=[hj1−1−μmhj2−1−μm⋯hjm−1−μmhj1−2−μm−1hj2−2−μm−1⋯hjm−2−μm−1⋱hj1−m−μ1hj2−m−μ1hjm−m−μ1].H_{[m],\{j_{1},j_{2},\cdots,j_{m}\}}=\begin{bmatrix}h_{j_{1}-1-\mu_{m}}&h_{j_{2}-1-\mu_{m}}&\cdots&h_{j_{m}-1-\mu_{m}}\\ h_{j_{1}-2-\mu_{m-1}}&h_{j_{2}-2-\mu_{m-1}}&\cdots&h_{j_{m}-2-\mu_{m-1}}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ h_{j_{1}-m-\mu_{1}}&h_{j_{2}-m-\mu_{1}}&\vdots&h_{j_{m}-m-\mu_{1}}\end{bmatrix}.

detH[m],{j1,j2,⋯,jm}=det[hjm−m−μ1hjm−m+1−μ2⋯hjm−1−μmhjm−1−m−μ1hjm−1−m+1−μ2⋯hjm−1−1−μm⋱hj1−m−μ1hj1−m+1−μ2hj1−1−μm]=sλ/μ,\det H_{[m],\{j_{1},j_{2},\cdots,j_{m}\}}=\det\begin{bmatrix}h_{j_{m}-m-\mu_{1}}&h_{j_{m}-m+1-\mu_{2}}&\cdots&h_{j_{m}-1-\mu_{m}}\\ h_{j_{m-1}-m-\mu_{1}}&h_{j_{m-1}-m+1-\mu_{2}}&\cdots&h_{j_{m-1}-1-\mu_{m}}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ h_{j_{1}-m-\mu_{1}}&h_{j_{1}-m+1-\mu_{2}}&\vdots&h_{j_{1}-1-\mu_{m}}\end{bmatrix}=s_{\lambda/\mu},

3.1 Toeplitz–Pfaffian Schur expansions

Let 𝐯=(v1,v2,…)\mathbf{v}=(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots) be commuting indeterminates, and define the infinite skew-symmetric matrix Ω⁡(𝐯)\Omega(\mathbf{v}) by

with all other entries equal to zero. Throughout this subsection, all infinite sums are interpreted coefficientwise with respect to the usual grading of the ring of symmetric functions.

Theorem 3.3.

For n≥1n\geq 1 and ℓ⁡(μ)≤2​n\ell(\mu)\leq 2n, we have

In this subsection, we present some applications of our main results. We first need the following lemma. Recall that H(n)=H∅(n)=[hj−i]1≤i≤n,j≥1H^{(n)}=H^{(n)}_{\varnothing}=\bigl[h_{j-i}\bigr]_{1\leq i\leq n,\ j\geq 1}.

Lemma 3.7.

Given p≥1p\geq 1, let Ω(p)​(𝐯)\Omega^{(p)}(\mathbf{v}) be an infinite skew-symmetric matrix defined in (8) with vi=0v_{i}=0 for i<pi<p and vi=ti−pv_{i}=t^{i-p} for i≥p.i\geq p. Let

By matrix multiplication,

Chen, Wang and Yang [7] proved the qq-log-convexity of the Narayana polynomials. Following their notation, one of the key steps is to prove the Schur positivity of D⁡(r)=∑k=0rD⁡(r,k,0,0),D(r)=\sum_{k=0}^{r}D(r,k,0,0), where

D⁡(r,k,0,0)=s(2k)​s(2r−k−1)+s(2k−1,12)​s(2r−k−1)−s(2k−1,1)​s(2r−k−1,1).D(r,k,0,0)=s_{(2^{k})}\,s_{(2^{r-k-1})}+s_{(2^{k-1},1^{2})}\,s_{(2^{r-k-1})}-s_{(2^{k-1},1)}\,s_{(2^{r-k-1},1)}.

See, for instance, [7, Section 3].

Corollary 3.9.

([7, Theorem 3.1]) For r≥1r\geq 1, the symmetric function D⁡(r)D(r) is Schur positive.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.1, it suffices to prove the Schur positivity of the standard involution

ω⁡(D⁡(r))=∑k=0r(s(k,k)​s(r−k−1,r−k−1)+s(k+1,k−1)​s(r−k−1,r−k−1)−s(k,k−1)​s(r−k,r−k−1)).\omega(D(r))=\sum_{k=0}^{r}\left(s_{(k,k)}\,s_{(r-k-1,r-k-1)}+s_{(k+1,k-1)}\,s_{(r-k-1,r-k-1)}-s_{(k,k-1)}\,s_{(r-k,r-k-1)}\right).

By the convolution formula for the coefficients of formal power series,

S(k,k)2=∑rtr​(∑k=0rs(k,k)​s(r−k,r−k))=∑rtr−1​(∑k=0r−1s(k,k)​s(r−k−1,r−k−1))S_{(k,k)}^{2}=\sum_{r}t^{r}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{r}s_{(k,k)}s_{(r-k,r-k)}\right)=\sum_{r}t^{r-1}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}s_{(k,k)}s_{(r-k-1,r-k-1)}\right)

Applying the same argument to the other two terms shows that ω⁡(D⁡(r))\omega(D(r)) equals the coefficient of tr−1t^{r-1} in

t⋅(S(k,k)​S(k+2,k)−S(k+1,k)2)+S(k,k)2.t\cdot\left(S_{(k,k)}S_{(k+2,k)}-S_{(k+1,k)}^{2}\right)+S_{(k,k)}^{2}.

By Theorem 3.8,

t⋅(S(k,k)​S(k+2,k)−S(k+1,k)2)+S(k,k)2=∑0≤b≤as(a,a,b,b)​ta+b.t\cdot\left(S_{(k,k)}S_{(k+2,k)}-S_{(k+1,k)}^{2}\right)+S_{(k,k)}^{2}=\sum_{0\leq b\leq a}s_{(a,a,b,b)}\,t^{a+b}.

Taking a=r−q−1a=r-q-1 and b=qb=q, we have

ω⁡(D⁡(r))=∑0≤q≤r−q−1s(r−q−1,r−q−1,q,q)=∑q=0⌊r−12⌋s(r−q−1,r−q−1,q,q),\omega(D(r))=\sum_{0\leq q\leq r-q-1}s_{(r-q-1,r-q-1,q,q)}=\sum_{q=0}^{\lfloor{\frac{r-1}{2}\rfloor}}s_{(r-q-1,r-q-1,q,q)},

and the Schur positivity of D⁡(r)D(r) follows. ∎

3.3 Vandermonde–Pfaffian Schur expansions

In this subsection, we show that Corollary 3.4 can be obtained by the earlier Schur–Pfaffian formulas of Ishikawa, Okada and Wakayama [21]. They combined the Pfaffian formula (1) with Vandermonde matrices. For an arbitrary skew-symmetric matrix A=[Ai​j]i,j≥1A=[A_{ij}]_{i,j\geq 1} and a Vandermonde matrix V=[xij−1]1≤i≤2​n,j≥1V=[x_{i}^{j-1}]_{1\leq i\leq 2n,\,j\geq 1}, the formula in [21, Theorem 2.3] states that

∑ℓ⁡(λ)≤2​nPf⁡(AJ⁡(λ),J⁡(λ))​sλ=1∏1≤r<s≤2​n(xs−xr)​Pf⁡(V​A​V𝖳),\sum_{\ell(\lambda)\leq 2n}\operatorname{Pf}\bigl(A_{J(\lambda),J(\lambda)}\bigr)s_{\lambda}=\frac{1}{\prod_{1\leq r<s\leq 2n}(x_{s}-x_{r})}\operatorname{Pf}\left(VAV^{\mathsf{T}}\right), (17)

where λ1≥λ2≥⋯≥λ2​n≥0\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\dots\geq\lambda_{2n}\geq 0 and

J⁡(λ)={λ2​n+1,λ2​n−1+2,…,λ2+2​n−1,λ1+2​n}<.J(\lambda)=\{\lambda_{2n}+1,\lambda_{2n-1}+2,\ldots,\lambda_{2}+2n-1,\lambda_{1}+2n\}_{<}.

Take A=Ω⁡(𝐯)A=\Omega(\mathbf{v}) for 𝐯=(1,t,t2,…).\mathbf{v}=(1,t,t^{2},\ldots). Then Ai,i+1=ti−1A_{i,i+1}=t^{i-1} and Ai+1,i=−ti−1,A_{i+1,i}=-t^{i-1}, with i≥1i\geq 1 and all other entries equal to 00. By the definition of the Pfaffian, Pf⁡(AJ⁡(λ),J⁡(λ))≠0\Pf\bigl(A_{J(\lambda),J(\lambda)}\bigr)\neq 0 if and only if

(λ2​n+1)+1=λ2​n−1+2,(λ2​n−2+3)+1=λ2​n−3+4,(λ2​n−4+5)+1=λ2​n−5+6,….(\lambda_{2n}+1)+1=\lambda_{2n-1}+2,\,(\lambda_{2n-2}+3)+1=\lambda_{2n-3}+4,\,(\lambda_{2n-4}+5)+1=\lambda_{2n-5}+6,\ldots.

Equivalently, λ2​n−2​k+2=λ2​n−2​k+1\lambda_{2n-2k+2}=\lambda_{2n-2k+1} for all 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n. In this case,

Pf⁡(AJ⁡(λ),J⁡(λ))=t∑k=1n((λ2​n−2​k+2+2​k−1)−1)=tn⁡(n−1)+∑k=1nλ2​n−2​k+2.\Pf\bigl(A_{J(\lambda),J(\lambda)}\bigr)=t^{\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left((\lambda_{2n-2k+2}+2k-1)-1\right)}=t^{n(n-1)+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\lambda_{2n-2k+2}}.

Let ak=λ2​n−2​k+2.a_{k}=\lambda_{2n-2k+2}. Then 0≤a1≤a2≤⋯≤an0\leq a_{1}\leq a_{2}\leq\dots\leq a_{n} and the left-hand side of (17) equals

∑0≤a1≤⋯≤ans(an2,an−12,…,a12)​tn⁡(n−1)+∑k=1nak.\sum_{0\leq a_{1}\leq\cdots\leq a_{n}}s_{(a^{2}_{n},a^{2}_{n-1},\ldots,a^{2}_{1})}\,t^{n(n-1)+\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_{k}}. (18)

Define the 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n matrix C=[Ci​j]1≤i,j≤2​nC=[C_{ij}]_{1\leq i,j\leq 2n} with

Ci​j=xj2​n−i∏1≤s≤2​ns≠j(xj−xs),C_{ij}=\frac{x_{j}^{2n-i}}{\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq s\leq 2n\\ s\neq j\end{subarray}}(x_{j}-x_{s})},

Proposition 3.11.

After specializing XX to the finite alphabet {x1,x2,…,x2​n}\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{2n}\}, we have

hm=∑r=12​nxrm+2​n−1∏1≤s≤2​ns≠r(xr−xs),h_{m}=\sum_{r=1}^{2n}\frac{x_{r}^{m+2n-1}}{\displaystyle\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq s\leq 2n\\ s\neq r\end{subarray}}(x_{r}-x_{s})},

4 Refined Baxter numbers and qq-refined Baxter numbers

In this section, we realize the refined and qq-refined Baxter numbers as principal specializations. Recall that

B⁡(n,k)=(nk)​(n+1k)​(n+2k)(k+1k)​(k+2k),0≤k≤n.B(n,k)=\frac{\binom{n}{k}\binom{n+1}{k}\binom{n+2}{k}}{\binom{k+1}{k}\binom{k+2}{k}},\quad 0\leq k\leq n.

Motivated by the definition of shifted qq-binomial coefficients and qq-Narayana numbers [3, 16], we define the qq-refined Baxter numbers as

Bq​(n,k)=q3​k​(k−1)2​[nk]q​[n+1k]q​[n+2k]q[k+1k]q​[k+2k]q,\displaystyle B_{q}(n,k)=q^{\frac{3k(k-1)}{2}}\frac{\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q}\begin{bmatrix}n+1\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q}\begin{bmatrix}n+2\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q}}{\begin{bmatrix}k+1\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q}\begin{bmatrix}k+2\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q}},

where

[k]q≔1−qk1−q,[k]q!≔[1]q[2]q⋯[k]q,[nk]q≔[n]q![k]q!​[n−k]q!.[k]_{q}\coloneqq\frac{1-q^{k}}{1-q},\qquad[k]_{q}!\coloneqq[1]_{q}[2]_{q}\cdots[k]_{q},\qquad\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q}\coloneqq\frac{[n]_{q}!}{[k]_{q}![n-k]_{q}!}.

For n≥0n\geq 0 and k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}, we adopt the convention

B⁡(n,k)=Bq​(n,k)=0unless0≤k≤n.B(n,k)=B_{q}(n,k)=0\quad\text{unless}\quad 0\leq k\leq n.

We remark that Cigler [10] defined a different qq-analogue of the refined Baxter numbers.

For a Schur function sλs_{\lambda}, its principal specialization is defined by

psn⁡(sλ)=sλ​(1,q,…,qn−1)andpsn1⁡(sλ)=sλ​(1n).\operatorname{ps}_{n}(s_{\lambda})=s_{\lambda}(1,q,\ldots,q^{n-1})\quad\textrm{and}\quad\operatorname{ps}^{1}_{n}(s_{\lambda})=s_{\lambda}(1^{n}).

In particular,

ps01⁡(sλ)={1,λ=∅,0,λ≠∅.\operatorname{ps}_{0}^{1}(s_{\lambda})=\begin{cases}1,&\lambda=\varnothing,\\ 0,&\lambda\neq\varnothing.\end{cases}

The following hook-content formula was first stated explicitly by Stanley [37].

Lemma 4.1.

[39, Theorem 7.21.2, Corollary 7.21.4] Let λ\lambda be a partition with at most nn parts. Then

psn⁡(sλ)=q∑i≥1(i−1)​λi​∏(i,j)∈λ1−qn+j−i1−qh⁡(i,j)\operatorname{ps}_{n}(s_{\lambda})=q^{\sum_{i\geq 1}(i-1)\lambda_{i}}\prod_{(i,j)\in\lambda}\frac{1-q^{n+j-i}}{1-q^{h(i,j)}}

and

psn1⁡(sλ)=∏(i,j)∈λn+j−ih⁡(i,j),\operatorname{ps}_{n}^{1}(s_{\lambda})=\prod_{(i,j)\in\lambda}\frac{n+j-i}{h(i,j)},

where h⁡(i,j)h(i,j) is the hook length of λ\lambda at (i,j)(i,j).

The following result is motivated by Cigler [10].

Lemma 4.2.

For n≥k≥0n\geq k\geq 0, we have Bq​(n,k)=psn⁡(s(3k))B_{q}(n,k)=\operatorname{ps}_{n}\left(s_{(3^{k})}\right).

Proof.

∑i≥1(i−1)​λi=3​k​(k−1)2andh⁡(i,j)=k−i−j+4.\sum_{i\geq 1}(i-1)\lambda_{i}=\frac{3k(k-1)}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad h(i,j)=k-i-j+4.

By Lemma 4.1, we deduce that

=q3​k​(k−1)2​∏i=1k∏j=13[n−i+j]q[k−i−j+4]q\displaystyle=q^{\frac{3k(k-1)}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\prod_{j=1}^{3}\frac{[n-i+j]_{q}}{[k-i-j+4]_{q}} (20)
=q3​k​(k−1)2​∏i=1k[n−i+1]q​[n−i+2]q​[n−i+3]q[k−i+1]q​[k−i+2]q​[k−i+3]q.\displaystyle=q^{\frac{3k(k-1)}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{[n-i+1]_{q}[n-i+2]_{q}[n-i+3]_{q}}{[k-i+1]_{q}[k-i+2]_{q}[k-i+3]_{q}}.

Since

5.1.2 The length-six terms

As stated in Section 5.1.1, for every term sμ​sνs_{\mu}s_{\nu} in ω⁡(∑k=0rF⁡(r,k))\omega\left(\sum_{k=0}^{r}F(r,k)\right), the length of each partition in its Littlewood–Richardson expansion is at most 66. For a partition λ=(λ1,…,λℓ⁡(λ))\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{\ell(\lambda)}), let

λ−=(λ1−1,…,λℓ⁡(λ)−1)\lambda^{-}=(\lambda_{1}-1,\ldots,\lambda_{\ell(\lambda)}-1)

denote the partition obtained by deleting the first column of its Young diagram, with zero parts omitted. Recall that cμ,νλc_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda} is the Littlewood–Richardson coefficient of sμ​sνs_{\mu}s_{\nu}. We introduce a result concerning cμ,νλc_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda} and cμ−,ν−λ−c_{\mu^{-},\nu^{-}}^{\lambda^{-}}.

Lemma 5.6.

[6, Lemma A.1] If cμ,νλ>0c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}>0 and ℓ⁡(λ)=ℓ⁡(μ)+ℓ⁡(ν)\ell(\lambda)=\ell(\mu)+\ell(\nu), then

Thus, in the maximal-length case, simultaneously deleting the first column from μ\mu, ν\nu, and λ\lambda preserves the corresponding Littlewood–Richardson coefficient. With a simple augmentation of Littlewood–Richardson tableaux, we obtain the following adding-column result.

Lemma 5.7.

Suppose that ℓ⁡(μ),ℓ⁡(ν)≤3\ell(\mu),\ell(\nu)\leq 3 and ℓ⁡(λ)≤6\ell(\lambda)\leq 6. Then for every d≥0d\geq 0,

cμ+(d3),ν+(d3)λ+(d6)=cμ,νλ.c_{\mu+(d^{3}),\nu+(d^{3})}^{\lambda+(d^{6})}=c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}.

cμ,νλ=cμ+(13),ν+(13)λ+(16).c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}=c_{\mu+(1^{3}),\nu+(1^{3})}^{\lambda+(1^{6})}.

Now we claim that if cμ+(13),ν+(13)λ+(16)=0c_{\mu+(1^{3}),\nu+(1^{3})}^{\lambda+(1^{6})}=0, then cμ,νλ=0c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}=0.

Assume, to the contrary, that cμ,νλ>0c_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}>0, and choose a Littlewood–Richardson tableau TT of shape λ/μ\lambda/\mu and content ν\nu. Add one column to the left of TT. The skew diagram

(λ+(16))/(μ+(13))({\lambda+(1^{6})})/({\mu+(1^{3})})

then has three additional cells, namely the cells in the first column of rows 4,5,64,5,6. Fill these cells with 1,2,31,2,3, respectively, and denote the resulting tableau by T+T^{+}.

The new first-column entries are strictly increasing. Moreover, since ℓ⁡(μ)≤3\ell(\mu)\leq 3, every old entry in row 55 is at least 22, and every old entry in row 66 is at least 33. 6 Log-convexity preservation and qq-log-concavity

In this section, we establish two further logarithmic properties associated with the refined Baxter numbers. We first prove that the Baxter transformation preserves log-convexity. We then study the qq-log-concavity of the qq-refined Baxter numbers in both the row and column directions, and extend these results to the qq-analogues of the dd-Hoggatt numbers.

6.1 The Baxter transformation

We show that the Baxter transformation preserves log-convexity. The qq-log-convexity of a polynomial sequence is closely related to the preservation of log-convexity by linear transformations. For a double-indexed sequence A⁡(n,k)A(n,k) with 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n and a sequence of nonnegative numbers (ak)k≥0,(a_{k})_{k\geq 0}, define

bn=∑k=0nA⁡(n,k)​ak.b_{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}A(n,k)a_{k}.

Note that in this section, the double-indexed sequence is indexed from 00 in both parameters. Liu and Wang [30] systematically studied linear transformations that preserve log-convexity. They proved that the linear transformations associated with many combinatorial numbers, such as the binomial coefficients, the Stirling numbers of the second kind and the Eulerian numbers preserve log-convexity, i.e., the log-convexity of (ak)k≥0(a_{k})_{k\geq 0} implies that of (bn)n≥0.(b_{n})_{n\geq 0}. See [8, 30, 42] for more details. Chen, Wang and Yang [7] subsequently proved that the linear transformation defined by the Narayana numbers preserves log-convexity. We present the following result.

Theorem 6.1.

If the sequence (ak)k≥0(a_{k})_{k\geq 0} of nonnegative real numbers is log-convex, then so is the sequence (bn)n≥0(b_{n})_{n\geq 0}, where

bn=∑k=0nB⁡(n,k)​ak,n≥0.b_{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}B(n,k)a_{k},\quad n\geq 0.

Following Liu and Wang [30, Section 4.2], it is not difficult to verify that for n≥1n\geq 1,

bn−1​bn+1−bn2=∑r=02​n(∑k=0⌊r/2⌋βk​(n,r)​ak​ar−k),b_{n-1}b_{n+1}-b_{n}^{2}=\sum_{r=0}^{2n}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\left\lfloor r/2\right\rfloor}\beta_{k}(n,r)a_{k}a_{r-k}\right), (32)

and

Bn−1​(x)​Bn+1​(x)−Bn​(x)2=∑r=02​n(∑k=0⌊r/2⌋βk​(n,r))​xr,B_{n-1}(x)B_{n+1}(x)-B_{n}(x)^{2}=\sum_{r=0}^{2n}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\left\lfloor r/2\right\rfloor}\beta_{k}(n,r)\right)x^{r}, (33)

where

βk​(n,r)={B⁡(n−1,k)​B​(n+1,r−k)+B⁡(n−1,r−k)​B​(n+1,k)−2​B​(n,k)​B​(n,r−k)if ​0≤k<r/2,B⁡(n−1,k)​B​(n+1,k)−B2​(n,k)if ​k=r/2.\beta_{k}(n,r)=\begin{cases}B(n-1,k)B(n+1,r-k)+B(n-1,r-k)B(n+1,k)\\ \qquad-2B(n,k)B(n,r-k)&\text{if }0\leq k<r/2,\\ B(n-1,k)B(n+1,k)-B^{2}(n,k)&\text{if }k=r/2.\end{cases}

Recall that

B⁡(n,k)=(nk)​(n+1k)​(n+2k)(k+1k)​(k+2k).B(n,k)=\frac{\binom{n}{k}\binom{n+1}{k}\binom{n+2}{k}}{\binom{k+1}{k}\binom{k+2}{k}}.

The following result can be obtained by direct computation; see [33, Theorem 2.3].

6.2 qq-Log-concavity

In this subsection, we prove the qq-log-concavity in both the row and column directions for the qq-refined Baxter numbers. Chen, Wang and Yang [7] established the qq-log-concavity of the qq-Narayana numbers. We prove the following results on the qq-refined Baxter numbers, in parallel to the results of qq-Narayana numbers.

Theorem 6.3.

Given an integer nn, the polynomial sequence (Bq​(n,k))0≤k≤n(B_{q}(n,k))_{0\leq k\leq n} is qq-log-concave.

Proof.

By Lemma 4.2, for any k≥1k\geq 1,

Bq​(n,k)2−Bq​(n,k−1)​Bq​(n,k+1)\displaystyle B_{q}(n,k)^{2}-B_{q}(n,k-1)B_{q}(n,k+1) =psn⁡(s(3k))​psn⁡(s(3k))−psn⁡(s(3k+1))​psn⁡(s(3k−1))\displaystyle=\operatorname{ps}_{n}\left(s_{(3^{k})}\right)\operatorname{ps}_{n}\left(s_{(3^{k})}\right)-\operatorname{ps}_{n}\left(s_{(3^{k+1})}\right)\operatorname{ps}_{n}\left(s_{(3^{k-1})}\right)
=psn⁡(s(3k)​s(3k)−s(3k+1)​s(3k−1)).\displaystyle=\operatorname{ps}_{n}\left(s_{(3^{k})}s_{(3^{k})}-s_{(3^{k+1})}s_{(3^{k-1})}\right).

Kirillov [26] proved that for a,b≥1a,b\geq 1, we have the following identity for Schur functions

s(ab)​s(ab)=s(ab+1)​s(ab−1)+s((a+1)b)​s((a−1)b).s_{(a^{b})}s_{(a^{b})}=s_{(a^{b+1})}s_{(a^{b-1})}+s_{((a+1)^{b})}s_{((a-1)^{b})}. (38)

Then

s(3k)​s(3k)−s(3k+1)​s(3k−1)=s(4k)​s(2k)s_{(3^{k})}s_{(3^{k})}-s_{(3^{k+1})}s_{(3^{k-1})}=s_{(4^{k})}s_{(2^{k})}

is Schur positive for any k≥0k\geq 0. Hence, the sequence (Bq​(n,k))0≤k≤n\left(B_{q}(n,k)\right)_{0\leq k\leq n} is qq-log-concave. ∎

The following is the qq-analogue of Lemma 6.2.

Theorem 6.4.

Given an integer kk, the polynomial sequence (Bq​(n,k))n≥k(B_{q}(n,k))_{n\geq k} is qq-log-concave.

We now turn to the qq-log-concavity of the qq-refined Baxter numbers for fixed kk. We first need the following result.

Lemma 6.5.

Let r,m,k≥0r,m,k\geq 0. Then

q−m​(r2)psk+3(s(mr))≥q0.q^{-m\binom{r}{2}}\operatorname{ps}_{k+3}\left(s_{(m^{r})}\right)\geq_{q}0.
Proof.

Note that if r>k+3r>k+3, then psk+3⁡(s(mr))=0,\operatorname{ps}_{k+3}(s_{(m^{r})})=0, and the assertion is immediate. We may therefore assume r≤k+3r\leq k+3. Using Lemma 4.1, we have

psk+3⁡(s(mr))=qm​(r2)​∏(i,j)∈(mr)1−qk+3+j−i1−qh⁡(i,j).\operatorname{ps}_{k+3}\left(s_{(m^{r})}\right)=q^{m\binom{r}{2}}\prod_{(i,j)\in(m^{r})}\frac{1-q^{k+3+j-i}}{1-q^{h(i,j)}}.

It is known [31, p. 44] that ∏(i,j)∈(mr)1−qk+3+j−i1−qh⁡(i,j)\prod_{(i,j)\in(m^{r})}\frac{1-q^{k+3+j-i}}{1-q^{h(i,j)}} is a polynomial in qq with nonnegative coefficients. Hence,

q−m​(r2)s(mr)(1,q,…,qk+2)=∏(i,j)∈(mr)1−qk+3+j−i1−qh⁡(i,j)≥q0.q^{-m\binom{r}{2}}s_{(m^{r})}(1,q,\ldots,q^{k+2})=\prod_{(i,j)\in(m^{r})}\frac{1-q^{k+3+j-i}}{1-q^{h(i,j)}}\geq_{q}0.

This completes the proof. ∎

6.3 qq-Analogue of the dd-Hoggatt numbers

Define the qq-analogue of the dd-Hoggatt numbers

Hq(d)​(n,k)=qd​k​(k−1)2​∏j=0d−1[n+jk]q[k+jk]q.H^{(d)}_{q}(n,k)=q^{\frac{dk(k-1)}{2}}\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{\begin{bmatrix}n+j\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q}}{\begin{bmatrix}k+j\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q}}.

In particular, when d=1,2d=1,2, and 33, Hq(d)​(n,k)H^{(d)}_{q}(n,k) specializes to the shifted qq-binomial coefficients, the qq-Narayana numbers, and the qq-refined Baxter numbers, respectively. By an argument analogous to the proof of Lemma 4.2, we can verify that

Hq(d)​(n,k)=psn⁡(s(dk)).H^{(d)}_{q}(n,k)=\operatorname{ps}_{n}\left(s_{(d^{k})}\right).

The following results generalize Theorems 6.3 and 6.4.

Theorem 6.6.

Given an integer nn, the polynomial sequence (Hq(d)​(n,k))0≤k≤n\left(H^{(d)}_{q}(n,k)\right)_{0\leq k\leq n} is qq-log-concave for any d≥1d\geq 1.

Proof.

The proof is similar to that of Theorem 6.3, with a=da=d in (38). ∎

Theorem 6.7.

Given an integer kk, the polynomial sequence (Hq(d)​(n,k))n≥k\left(H^{(d)}_{q}(n,k)\right)_{n\geq k} is qq-log-concave for any d≥1d\geq 1.

Proof.

Recall that Hq(d)​(k+m,k)H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m,k) equals

psk+m⁡(s(dk))=qd​k​(k−1)2​∏j=0d−1[k+m+jk]q[k+jk]q=qd​k​(k−1)2​∏j=0d−1[k+m+j]q!​[j]q![k+j]q!​[m+j]q!.\operatorname{ps}_{k+m}\left(s_{(d^{k})}\right)=q^{\frac{dk(k-1)}{2}}\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{\begin{bmatrix}k+m+j\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q}}{\begin{bmatrix}k+j\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q}}=q^{\frac{dk(k-1)}{2}}\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{[k+m+j]_{q}![j]_{q}!}{[k+j]_{q}![m+j]_{q}!}.

By Lemma 4.1, the hook-content formula gives

psk+d⁡(s(md))=qm​(d2)​∏i=1d∏j=1m[k+d+j−i]q[m+d−i−j+1]q.\operatorname{ps}_{k+d}\left(s_{(m^{d})}\right)=q^{m\binom{d}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{d}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\frac{[k+d+j-i]_{q}}{[m+d-i-j+1]_{q}}.

Reversing the index ii and rearranging the products, we obtain

psk+d⁡(s(md))=qm​(d2)​∏j=0d−1[k+m+j]q!​[j]q![k+j]q!​[m+j]q!.\operatorname{ps}_{k+d}\left(s_{(m^{d})}\right)=q^{m\binom{d}{2}}\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{[k+m+j]_{q}![j]_{q}!}{[k+j]_{q}![m+j]_{q}!}.

Therefore,

Hq(d)​(k+m,k)=qd​k​(k−1)2−m​(d2)​psk+d⁡(s(md)).H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m,k)=q^{\frac{dk(k-1)}{2}-m\binom{d}{2}}\operatorname{ps}_{k+d}\left(s_{(m^{d})}\right).

It is obvious that

Hq(d)(k,k)2=qd​k​(k−1)≥q0.H_{q}^{(d)}(k,k)^{2}=q^{dk(k-1)}\geq_{q}0.

For m≥1m\geq 1, we have

Hq(d)​(k+m,k)2−Hq(d)​(k+m−1,k)​Hq(d)​(k+m+1,k)\displaystyle H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m,k)^{2}-H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m-1,k)H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m+1,k)
=\displaystyle={} qd​k​(k−1)−d⁡(d−1)​m​psk+d⁡(s(md)2−s((m−1)d)​s((m+1)d)).\displaystyle q^{dk(k-1)-d(d-1)m}\operatorname{ps}_{k+d}\left(s_{(m^{d})}^{2}-s_{((m-1)^{d})}s_{((m+1)^{d})}\right).

Taking a=m,b=da=m,b=d in (38), Hq(d)​(k+m,k)2−Hq(d)​(k+m−1,k)​Hq(d)​(k+m+1,k)H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m,k)^{2}-H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m-1,k)H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m+1,k) equals

qd​k​(k−1)−d⁡(d−1)​m​psk+d⁡(s(md−1)​s(md+1)).q^{dk(k-1)-d(d-1)m}\operatorname{ps}_{k+d}\left(s_{(m^{d-1})}s_{(m^{d+1})}\right).

By the same argument as in the proof of Lemma 6.5, we can obtain

q−m​(d−12)psk+d(s(md−1))≥q0andq−m​(d+12)psk+d(s(md+1))≥q0.q^{-m\binom{d-1}{2}}\operatorname{ps}_{k+d}\left(s_{(m^{d-1})}\right)\geq_{q}0\quad\textrm{and}\quad q^{-m\binom{d+1}{2}}\operatorname{ps}_{k+d}\left(s_{(m^{d+1})}\right)\geq_{q}0.

Consequently, Hq(d)​(k+m,k)2−Hq(d)​(k+m−1,k)​Hq(d)​(k+m+1,k)H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m,k)^{2}-H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m-1,k)H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m+1,k) equals

qd​k​(k−1)+m​(q−m​(d−12)​psk+d⁡(s(md−1)))​(q−m​(d+12)​psk+d⁡(s(md+1))).q^{dk(k-1)+m}\left(q^{-m\binom{d-1}{2}}\operatorname{ps}_{k+d}\left(s_{(m^{d-1})}\right)\right)\left(q^{-m\binom{d+1}{2}}\operatorname{ps}_{k+d}\left(s_{(m^{d+1})}\right)\right).

Then for d≥1d\geq 1, we have

Hq(d)(k+m,k)2−Hq(d)(k+m−1,k)Hq(d)(k+m+1,k)≥q0.H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m,k)^{2}-H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m-1,k)H_{q}^{(d)}(k+m+1,k)\geq_{q}0.

Thus, for any fixed kk, the sequence (Hq(d)​(n,k))n≥k\left(H_{q}^{(d)}(n,k)\right)_{n\geq k} is qq-log-concave. ∎

Appendix B Auxiliary symmetric-function identities

Lemma B.1.

We have

e2​S(k,k)−e1​S(k+1,k)\displaystyle e_{2}S_{(k,k)}-e_{1}S_{(k+1,k)} =S(k,k,1,1)−S(k+2,k),\displaystyle=S_{(k,k,1,1)}-S_{(k+2,k)}, (39)
e2​S(k+1,k)−e1​S(k+2,k)\displaystyle e_{2}S_{(k+1,k)}-e_{1}S_{(k+2,k)} =S(k+1,k,1,1)+S(k,k,1)t−S(k+3,k).\displaystyle=S_{(k+1,k,1,1)}+\frac{S_{(k,k,1)}}{t}-S_{(k+3,k)}. (40)
Proof.

By vertical Pieri’s rule (Theorem 2.2), we have

e2​s(k,k)=s(k+1,k+1)+s(k+1,k,1)+s(k,k,1,1),e_{2}s_{(k,k)}=s_{(k+1,k+1)}+s_{(k+1,k,1)}+s_{(k,k,1,1)},
e1​s(k+1,k)=s(k+2,k)+s(k+1,k+1)+s(k+1,k,1).e_{1}s_{(k+1,k)}=s_{(k+2,k)}+s_{(k+1,k+1)}+s_{(k+1,k,1)}.

Subtracting these two identities, multiplying by tkt^{k} and summing over k≥0k\geq 0 yields

e2​S(k,k)−e1​S(k+1,k)=S(k,k,1,1)−S(k+2,k).e_{2}S_{(k,k)}-e_{1}S_{(k+1,k)}=S_{(k,k,1,1)}-S_{(k+2,k)}.

Similarly,

e2​s(k+1,k)=s(k+2,k+1)+s(k+2,k,1)+s(k+1,k+1,1)+s(k+1,k,1,1),e_{2}s_{(k+1,k)}=s_{(k+2,k+1)}+s_{(k+2,k,1)}+s_{(k+1,k+1,1)}+s_{(k+1,k,1,1)},
e1​s(k+2,k)=s(k+3,k)+s(k+2,k+1)+s(k+2,k,1).e_{1}s_{(k+2,k)}=s_{(k+3,k)}+s_{(k+2,k+1)}+s_{(k+2,k,1)}.

Therefore,

e2​s(k+1,k)−e1​s(k+2,k)=s(k+1,k+1,1)+s(k+1,k,1,1)−s(k+3,k).e_{2}s_{(k+1,k)}-e_{1}s_{(k+2,k)}=s_{(k+1,k+1,1)}+s_{(k+1,k,1,1)}-s_{(k+3,k)}.

Multiplying by tkt^{k} and summing over k≥0k\geq 0, and using S(k,k,1)/t=∑k≥0s(k+1,k+1,1)​tk,{S_{(k,k,1)}}/{t}=\sum_{k\geq 0}s_{(k+1,k+1,1)}\,t^{k}, we have

e2​S(k+1,k)−e1​S(k+2,k)=S(k,k,1)t+S(k+1,k,1,1)−S(k+3,k).e_{2}S_{(k+1,k)}-e_{1}S_{(k+2,k)}=\frac{S_{(k,k,1)}}{t}+S_{(k+1,k,1,1)}-S_{(k+3,k)}.

This completes the proof. ∎

We present two further identities that will be used in the proof of (16).

Lemma B.2.

We have

S(k+3,k)=e3​S(k,k)−e2​S(k+1,k)+e1​S(k+2,k)−S(k,k,1,1,1).S_{(k+3,k)}=e_{3}S_{(k,k)}-e_{2}S_{(k+1,k)}+e_{1}S_{(k+2,k)}-S_{(k,k,1,1,1)}. (41)
S(k,k,2,2)\displaystyle S_{(k,k,2,2)} =S(k,k)−1t2+h2​S(k,k)−e1​S(k+1,k)t+e2​S(k+2,k)\displaystyle=\frac{S_{(k,k)}-1}{t^{2}}+\frac{h_{2}S_{(k,k)}-e_{1}S_{(k+1,k)}}{t}+e_{2}S_{(k+2,k)} (42)
−(e1h2−h3)⋅S(k+1,k)+(h22−e1h3)⋅S(k,k).\displaystyle\qquad-(e_{1}h_{2}-h_{3})\cdot S_{(k+1,k)}+(h_{2}^{2}-e_{1}h_{3})\cdot S_{(k,k)}.
Proof.

By vertical Pieri’s rule (Theorem 2.2),

e3​s(k,k)=s(k+1,k+1,1)+s(k+1,k,1,1)+s(k,k,1,1,1),e1​s(k+2,k)=s(k+3,k)+s(k+2,k+1)+s(k+2,k,1),e_{3}s_{(k,k)}=s_{(k+1,k+1,1)}+s_{(k+1,k,1,1)}+s_{(k,k,1,1,1)},\quad e_{1}s_{(k+2,k)}=s_{(k+3,k)}+s_{(k+2,k+1)}+s_{(k+2,k,1)},
e2​s(k+1,k)=s(k+2,k+1)+s(k+2,k,1)+s(k+1,k+1,1)+s(k+1,k,1,1).e_{2}s_{(k+1,k)}=s_{(k+2,k+1)}+s_{(k+2,k,1)}+s_{(k+1,k+1,1)}+s_{(k+1,k,1,1)}.

Thus,

and equation (41) follows.

−(e1​h2−h3)​s(k+1,k)+(h22−e1​h3)​s(k,k).\displaystyle-(e_{1}h_{2}-h_{3})s_{(k+1,k)}+(h_{2}^{2}-e_{1}h_{3})s_{(k,k)}.

By Pieri’s rule,

+s(k+2,k,2)+s(k+2,k,1,1)+s(k+1,k+1,2)+s(k+1,k+1,1,1)+s(k+1,k,2,1),\displaystyle+s_{(k+2,k,2)}+s_{(k+2,k,1,1)}+s_{(k+1,k+1,2)}+s_{(k+1,k+1,1,1)}+s_{(k+1,k,2,1)},

+s(k+1,k+1,1,1)+s(k+1,k,2,1)+s(k,k,2,2).\displaystyle+s_{(k+1,k+1,1,1)}+s_{(k+1,k,2,1)}+s_{(k,k,2,2)}.

Substitution and cancellation yield [tk]​R=s(k,k,2,2).[t^{k}]R=s_{(k,k,2,2)}. This completes the proof. ∎
